note_out: The overview links panpsychism's revival to the hard problem and identifies Chalmers as treating it as viable.
The page identifies Hofstadter and Dennett as co-editors and co-authors of The Mind's I.
Koch describes his NCC work with Crick and subsequent integrated-information work with Tononi.
Baars explicitly says GWT views the brain as a society of mind made of specialized, mostly unconscious processors.
The article explicitly compares Freud's unconscious primary process with Kahneman's largely unconscious System 1.
Seth identifies Damasio's framework as related and grounds feeling and selfhood in interoception and physiological homeostasis.
Hoffman acknowledges similar idealist ideas, then explicitly says MUI theory is not idealism.
Blackmore's illusionist account explicitly cites Metzinger when describing a temporary self-model of a continuing observer.
The influence section says Leary found the book corroborated his psilocybin experience, arranged a meeting, and became friendly with Huxley.
The page discusses both Pribram's quantum-field holonomic theory and Penrose-Hameroff Orch-OR as quantum-mind proposals.
Egan's synopsis describes conscious software copies of brains running in virtual reality.
Bach's dissertation devotes comparative sections to Soar and ACT-R and contrasts their scope with Psi/MicroPsi.
Bach explicitly says Maslow's hierarchy of needs is better understood as a hierarchy of purposes.
Bach states that Dörner's blueprint incorporates Bischof's ideas and discusses Bischof's cybernetic treatment of psychological feedback loops.
Bach explicitly contrasts OCC's implemented emotion categories with MicroPsi emotions emerging from whole-system modulator configurations.
In the methodology section, Bach cites Sloman for understanding minds through the active design stance of a constructing engineer.
At 22:47, Bach explains motivation cybernetically: needs are balanced by a homeostatic control system.
Bach cites Schank and Abelson for hierarchical scripts, then supplies a neural implementation for sensorimotor script execution.
In section 1, Bach lists Baars's GWT as a functional approach whose explanation converges on phenomenal consciousness.
Bach says the self is a model, not an agent, and explicitly directs readers to Metzinger's Being No One.
Bach explicitly calls Cortical Conductor Theory an extension of Dennett's multiple-drafts model.
At 1:26:49, Vervaeke calls Plato's cave the first simulation theory; Bach answers, “Almost.”
At 00:21:49, Bach says stage-six enlightenment is found mostly among advanced Buddhist meditators.
At 11:28–12:53, Bach calls Chalmers's hard problem a misunderstanding and explains experience as a mind-created world.
At 37:23–37:54, Bach says physical things cannot be conscious; only suitable representational software structures can dream.
In the daytime-dream passage, Bach says waking neocortical simulation uses dream circuitry but is constrained by sensory input.
At 38:03–38:36, Bach attributes to Levin the hypothesis that morphogenesis and mind use the same coherence algorithm.
At 00:38–00:44, the discussion explicitly moves from Dawkins's gene competition to Bach's competing software agents.
At 2:36:30–2:36:54, Bach describes Greek gods as cross-mind psychological archetypes.
Bach describes Christianity awakening as a societal agent, with the Catholic Church as its nervous system and brain.
Bach discusses gods as mental constructs and cross-mind selves, but no opened source tied this account to Jaynes.
Early in the talk, Bach says the universe produces regular patterns and therefore necessarily and sufficiently is a computer.
Near the opening, Bach credits La Mettrie with humans as mathematical machines; elsewhere he calls computationalism the new mechanism.
Bach strongly advocates constructive mathematics, but no opened source documented a specific debt to Brouwer or intuitionism.
In the mathematics-foundations section, Bach starts with Cantor's sets, then rejects completed infinities as unconstructible.
Bach defends Church–Turing universality and doubts physical hypercomputers, but the categorical note is stronger than the opened passages.
Bach presents the Tractatus as Wittgenstein's attempt to reverse-engineer thought into a precise, formal language.
Bach explicitly derives faith, love, and hope as Aquinas's three divine virtues for forming a higher-level agent.
In the ethics section, Bach critiques utilitarian aggregation of hedonic states and derives ethics from negotiations among agents.
From 01:14 onward, Bach explains language models as representational-state transition functions, useful but ungrounded components of larger systems.
The event page lists Bach and Shanahan as featured speakers on the same machine-sentience panel.
Appendix B cites Butlin et al. while describing nonprofit research on AI moral patienthood and welfare.
The Bach-authored essay grounds CIMC's hypothesis in computational functionalism, conductor theory, and consciousness arising near the beginning of development.
The whitepaper says IIT denies consciousness to a functionally perfect digital brain simulation when its hardware causal architecture differs.
